title: How Bias Gets into AI

thumbnail.headline: Where Does Bias Start?
thumbnail.image: Navy background, three glowing doorways labelled by icons (a database, a blueprint, a hand) with a thin red thread running through them, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Where Does Bias Start?
slide.body: Three doorway icons in a row: data (stack of records), design (blueprint), use (hand pressing a button), joined by a red thread. Small tag: AI Ethics, Bias and Safety · Lesson 2.

production_notes: No facts to verify: the CV-screening and loan examples are hypothetical on purpose, with no real companies, incidents or statistics (content.md Review Flags: None).
Claire Tremblay and her engineering company in Canada are fictional; stock footage must not show a real company name or logo, and CVs on screen must use invented placeholder details only.

Hook.voiceover: Nobody sits down and writes treat women worse, or ignore rural customers, into an AI system. Yet biased systems appear again and again. If nobody plans the bias, where does it come from?

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you met bias. Results that are better or worse for some groups. Bias rarely comes from one bad decision. It usually enters quietly, at one or more of three points. The data, the design, and the use.

slide.title: Three ways in
slide.body: Three boxes in a row, revealed one by one: 1 Data · 2 Design · 3 Use, each with an arrow into a central 'AI system' box.

Explain.voiceover: First, the data. An AI system learns patterns from examples. If the examples are unbalanced, the patterns will be too. Some groups may be missing, like darker skin in a skin-condition app. Some may be over-represented, like city speakers in a speech tool. And if past decisions were unfair, the data records that unfairness as if it were correct.

slide.title: 1. The data
slide.body: Missing groups: few photos of darker skin · Over-represented groups: mostly city speakers · Past unfairness recorded as 'correct'

Explain.voiceover: Second, the design. People decide what the system should predict, and which details it may use. A tool that predicts who will cost the most is not the same as one that predicts who needs the most care. And even if the system never sees gender, details like a postcode or a gap in employment can stand in for it. We call these proxies.

slide.title: 2. The design
slide.body: Left: Target 'who will cost the most' vs Right: 'who needs the most care'. Below: Proxies: postcode · school name · career gap → can stand in for gender or background.

Explain.voiceover: Third, the use. A system can be fair in one place and unfair in another. It may be used for a different purpose, or in a group it was never tested on. And people may trust it too much and stop checking.
Explain.stock_query: office worker clicking approve without reading

Explain.voiceover: Here is a simple picture. A recipe copied from an old cookbook repeats its mistakes, however carefully you cook. If the cookbook used too much salt, your dish will be too salty, even if you measure perfectly. Careful training cannot fix mistakes that were already in the recipe.
Explain.stock_query: cook reading old recipe book kitchen

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's follow one example. Claire Tremblay leads recruitment at an engineering company in Canada. To save time, the company builds a CV-screening tool, trained on ten years of past hires. CVs of people who were hired are labelled good, and all the others are labelled not selected. It sounds sensible. Let's see what happens.
Demonstrate.stock_query: recruiter reviewing job applications on laptop

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now watch the three points. The data: most engineers hired in those ten years were men from three local universities, so the tool learns that CVs like theirs are good. The design: the team asked it to predict people like our past hires, not people who will do the job well. It also reads hobbies and clubs, which can act as proxies.

slide.title: How bias entered
slide.body: Data: ten years of hires, mostly men from three universities → Design: target 'people like our past hires' + hobbies and clubs as proxies → (Use appears next)

Demonstrate.voiceover: The use: recruiters start to trust the tool's top twenty list and stop reading the other CVs. Qualified people from other universities, and many women, are never seen by a person. Nobody wanted this. But the tool now repeats old hiring patterns at high speed.

slide.title: The use
slide.body: Stack of CVs: top 20 highlighted and read; the rest greyed out and never opened. Caption: old patterns, repeated at speed.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Claire's team makes three changes. They check which groups are in the training data. They change the goal to match the skills in the job description. And a person reviews a sample of rejected CVs every week.

slide.title: Three fixes
slide.body: Check who is in the data · Target = skills in the job description · Weekly human review of rejected CVs

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to think that removing names, gender or age makes a system fair. Other details can still act as proxies, A women's sports club, a school for girls, or a career gap for childcare can all carry the same pattern. So removing details can be one step, but you still need to test results for different groups, as you will learn later in this course.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, bias can enter through the data, the design and the use. Second, data that records past decisions can also record past unfairness, and the system learns it as if it were correct. Third, removing names or gender is not enough, because other details can act as proxies. Results must be tested. Keep these three points in mind whenever you meet a new AI tool.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Bias enters through data, design and use. 2. Past decisions can carry past unfairness. 3. Proxies remain: always test results.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will look at a loan-approval model at a bank in Kenya, and list one way bias could enter through the data, the design and the use. It takes about fifteen minutes. In the next lesson, we will look at fairness, and who gets helped and who gets hurt. See you there.
